judge.reason: The submitted answer only says the answer is unknown, without stating any established bounds or other mathematical information. It therefore makes no qualifying claim and matches none of the listed answers.

options.counterfactual: An Oka domain can have a strongly pseudoconvex boundary point when its defining function is negative inside the domain.
options.approach: Recheck the local peak-function construction, focusing on whether its strict negativity holds uniformly on the artificial boundary. Identify the precise inequality that prevents extending the truncated function plurisubharmonically.

options.counterfactual: An Oka domain can have a strongly pseudoconvex boundary point when its defining function is negative inside the domain.
options.approach: Search for an explicit Oka domain with compact complement and such a boundary point. If the example occurs in complex dimension two and satisfies the required smoothness, use it to disprove membership of that dimension in N.

options.counterfactual: An Oka domain can have a strongly pseudoconvex boundary point when its defining function is negative inside the domain.
options.approach: Revisit the consequence of convex approximation for bounded plurisubharmonic functions. Check whether approximation supplies the entire maps and local domination needed for the claimed obstruction.

options.counterfactual: There is a general theorem that the complement of every smoothly bounded pseudoconvex compact domain in complex Euclidean space is Oka, without polynomial convexity or a Stein neighbourhood basis.
options.approach: Formulate the theorem with its precise dimensional and boundary-regularity hypotheses, then compare each hypothesis with the definition of K_n. Use that comparison to determine S.

options.counterfactual: There is a general theorem that the complement of every smoothly bounded pseudoconvex compact domain in complex Euclidean space is Oka, without polynomial convexity or a Stein neighbourhood basis.
options.approach: Investigate whether the theorem also covers compact obstacles with mixed Levi signature. Such an extension could provide counterexamples to the necessity implication in dimensions at least three.

options.counterfactual: There is a general theorem that the complement of every smoothly bounded pseudoconvex compact domain in complex Euclidean space is Oka, without polynomial convexity or a Stein neighbourhood basis.
options.approach: Examine how the theorem handles smoothly bounded pseudoconvex domains lacking a Stein neighbourhood basis. Understanding that step would distinguish the general result from the familiar polynomially convex complement theorem.

options.counterfactual: In every complex dimension, the Oka property of the complement forces the compact obstacle to have pseudoconvex boundary, even when a failure of pseudoconvexity has mixed Levi signature.
options.approach: Seek an obstruction stronger than bounded plurisubharmonic functions that follows from convex approximation and detects a single negative Levi direction of the obstacle. Apply it locally at a mixed-signature boundary point.

options.counterfactual: In every complex dimension, the Oka property of the complement forces the compact obstacle to have pseudoconvex boundary, even when a failure of pseudoconvexity has mixed Levi signature.
options.approach: Investigate a reduction to a two-dimensional complex slice containing a negative Levi direction and the complex normal. Determine what additional approximation argument would transfer the two-dimensional obstruction to the full complement without assuming slices of Oka manifolds are Oka.

options.counterfactual: In every complex dimension, the Oka property of the complement forces the compact obstacle to have pseudoconvex boundary, even when a failure of pseudoconvexity has mixed Levi signature.
options.approach: Use a smooth compact Hartogs obstacle with mixed Levi signature as a test case. Try to construct a holomorphic map on a convex compact set that cannot be approximated by entire maps avoiding the obstacle.
